Network Flow

Explore network flow through course notes, diagnostic assessment, practice and exam-style questions.

Focus: directed networks, source and sink, flow conservation, maximum flow, minimum cuts, capacity changes and arrow direction. Includes multi-stage networks with up to nine vertices. Year 12 Mathematics Standard 2.

Network Flow course notes

Clear explanations, key formulas and worked examples.

Key terms
Cut (networks)
Partition separating source from sink.
Directed network
Network with arrows specifying direction.
Edge (networks)
Connection between vertices.
Flow capacity
Maximum permitted flow on an edge or network.
Inflow (networks)
Actual flow entering a vertex.
Maximum-flow minimum-cut theorem
Maximum feasible flow equals minimum cut capacity.
Minimum cut
Source–sink cut with least capacity.
Outflow (networks)
Actual flow leaving a vertex.
Sink (networks)
Destination receiving flow.
Source (networks)
Origin supplying flow.

Diagnostic Test

24 multiple-choice questions: 8 foundations and 16 topic knowledge. Submit for separate scores and explanations.

Skill Practice

Build fluency with key ideas before attempting extended exam questions. Reveal the answers when ready.

1. Conservation at a junction

Two roads bring 12 and 9 vehicles per minute into a junction. One road carries 8 vehicles per minute out. Find the flow in the other outgoing road.

13 vehicles/min. Total inflow = 12 + 9 = 21, so 21 − 8 = 13.

2. Series bottleneck

Three stages can process 18, 14 and 20 parcels per hour. Find the maximum steady throughput.

14 parcels/hour. The slowest stage limits the whole process.

3. Cut capacity

Three directed arcs cross from the source side of a cut to the sink side with capacities 4, 7 and 6. Find the cut capacity.

17 units. Add capacities of arcs crossing the cut in the forward direction.

4. Flow versus capacity

An arc has capacity 11 units/min and currently carries 8 units/min. How much additional flow can it carry?

3 units/min. Residual forward capacity = 11 − 8.

Worked Examples

Step-by-step models for common exam question types.

Example 1 · Conservation of flow

At a junction, incoming flows are 16 and 11 L/s. One outgoing pipe carries 9 L/s. Find the other outgoing flow.

Step 1: Inflow = outflow, assuming no loss or storage.

Step 2: 16 + 11 = 9 + x.

Step 3: x = 18 L/s.

Example 2 · Maximum flow and a minimum cut

A network has arcs S→A (6), S→B (5), A→T (4), A→B (2) and B→T (7).

Step 1: Send 4 along S→A→T, 2 along S→A→B→T and 5 along S→B→T.

Step 2: Total feasible flow = 4 + 2 + 5 = 11.

Step 3: The cut {S}|{A,B,T} has capacity 6 + 5 = 11.

Conclusion: Maximum flow is 11, since a feasible flow equals a cut capacity.

Spot the Mistake

Identify the incorrect reasoning before revealing the explanation.

Mistake 1 · Adding every capacity

A student says: “The maximum flow is the sum of all capacities anywhere in the network.” Explain the mistake.

Arcs within a network cannot all be added: units may travel along multiple arcs and would be counted more than once. Flow must obey capacities and conservation. A minimum cut can establish an upper bound.

Mistake 2 · Ignoring arrow directions

A student includes an arc pointing from the sink side back to the source side when calculating the capacity of a directed cut. Explain the error.

For a directed S–T cut, add only capacities of arcs directed from the source-side set to the sink-side set, not reverse-direction arcs.

Mistake 3 · Confusing capacity with flow

An arc is labelled with capacity 9. A student claims that 9 units must always travel along it. Explain.

Capacity is an upper limit. The actual flow can be any feasible amount from 0 up to 9, subject to the rest of the network.
